newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Portugal, Indonesia clash at U.N. over East Timor.
newsitem.headline: Portugal, Indonesia clash at U.N. over East Timor.

text.p: Portugal and Indonesia clashed in a U.N. committee on Tuesday over the question of East Timor, two days before their foreign ministers were scheduled to hold another in a protracted series of U.N.-sponsored meetings on the issue.
Indonesia occupied East Timor in 1975 after Portugal withdrew from its former colony. The territory was incorporated the following year as Indonesia's 27th province.
But this was not recognised by the international community and talks between Portugal and Indonesia to find an internationally acceptable solution have dragged on since 1983, under U.N. auspices.

The foreign ministers of the two countries are to meet at the United Nations on June 19-20 for a ninth round of talks -- the first since Secretary-General Kofi Annan took office in January and appointed former Pakistani U.N. representative Jamsheed Marker as his personal representative for East Timor.

Addressing the U.N. decolonization committee, ambassador Fernando Neves of Portugal said: "East Timor's decolonization process was brutally interrupted by Indonesia's military invasion in 1975 and since then it has been prevented by Indonesia's illegal occupation of the territory."

He accused Indonesia of retaining an excessive military and security presence in East Timor and cited various sources as reporting a "persistent pattern of arbitrary arrests, interrogation and torture."

"The outburst of violence that was witnessed during the recent illegal elections imposed on the people of East Timor by the Indonesian occupants shows that, as long as their right to self-determination is not recognised, the East Timorese will not give up their fight."

Neves said a just solution could be found only if the parties approached the U.N.-sponsored negotiations in good faith, without preconceived ideas and with an open mind, "and if they recognise that only the people of East Timor have the right to determine their own future."
"It is in this spirit that Portugal will approach the next round of negotiations, scheduled for later this week."

Marty Natalegawa of Indonesia, replying to what he called the Poruguese envoy's "unwarranted allegations and misrepresentations," said the territory was decolonized when its people "opted for independence through integration with Indonesia."

This was an exercise of their right of self-determination, in conformity with U.N. resolutions and their traditional democratic practices, and was witnessed by scores of members of the diplomatic corps and local and international media.

"Today, it is astonishing that Portugal proclaims itself as the so-called champion of self-determination and human rights when its past record in this field ... is known to be the worst in the annals of decolinization," Natalegawa said.

He called allegations of torture, detentions and killing "an outrage," adding: "Indonesia is a law-abiding society, committed to upholding its laws as well as according due process of law to all its citizens."

He said East Timor had made "vast strides" in its economic, political and social development, as well as in the religious and cultural sectors, and its infrastructure "bears no resemblance to its tragic colonial past."
